title: Phase Diagram Infographic
creator: Dan McCreary
subject: AP Chemistry
description: Interactive pressure-temperature phase diagrams of water and carbon dioxide, side by side or overlaid, with labeled regions, triple and critical points, zoom insets showing the slope of each solid-liquid curve, and a movable probe that reports the phase of each substance.

learningObjectives: Locate and interpret the triple point, critical point, and phase regions on a phase diagram
Classify the phase of a substance at a given temperature and pressure
Explain how the slope of water's solid-liquid boundary differs from that of most substances
standards: AP Chemistry CED Unit 3: Intermolecular Forces and Properties (properties of solids, liquids, and gases)

controls.label: Probe
controls.description: Click or drag on a diagram to set the temperature and pressure; the probe snaps to curves and marked points

controls.label: Overlay Both Diagrams
controls.description: Toggles between side by side diagrams and both substances on one set of axes

controls.label: Jump to
controls.description: Moves the probe to a notable point such as room conditions or a triple point

equations: Water liquid-gas: Wagner and Pruss saturation-pressure equation (IAPWS-95)
Water solid-gas and solid-liquid: IAPWS 2011 sublimation and melting pressure equations for ice Ih
Carbon dioxide: Span and Wagner (1996) vapor-pressure, sublimation-pressure, and melting-pressure equations
assumptions: Only ice Ih is shown for water; the pressure axis stops near 2000 atm
Pressure axis is logarithmic; zoom insets use a linear pressure axis

pedagogical.teachingStrategy: Probe-and-classify exploration with side by side comparison
keyQuestions: Why does dry ice sublime instead of melting at atmospheric pressure?
What does increasing the pressure do to the melting point of ice, and why is that unusual?
What happens to the difference between liquid and gas beyond the critical point?
commonMisconceptions: Believing every substance has a liquid phase at 1 atm
Believing higher pressure always raises the melting point
Treating the critical point as a third boundary rather than the end of the liquid-gas curve
assessmentOpportunities: Have students predict the phase of each substance at a stated temperature and pressure, then check with the probe
